review:
I don't understand why this game was so harshly criticized by many reviewers. From my point of view it's by far one of the best games I've played and I would definitely recommend it to everyone to play it. It's a shame the sequel won't be released as it would have had huge potential.

The story was very engaging, and also long which is not easy to achieve. There aren't many open world games with such a long story and so many characters, characters that have been thought out in such a way that they each have a story behind them and a role in the story of the game, where you care about them and are not just for filler. The only thing that can get boring is that if you want to max the level of the camps for different weapons upgrades or for the motorcycle you have to do some repetitive things but personally I didn't mind this because I did them progresivly during the story. I like that they implemented the hordes, an original idea that is both fun and scary, especially scary at the beginning of the game when you don't have the right equipment.

On the graphics side, it has beautiful graphics and looks very good in combination with an HDR monitor and I especially like that in photo mode you can make many advanced settings exactly as you would do on cameras in real life. I didn't have any optimization problems at all and the game ran very fluently at a high frame rate, but some time has passed since the launch and usually the problems related to optimization are solved shortly after the launch of a game ( The only thing that isn't really a problem but is an optimization error would be that sometimes when I fast traveled to any of the camps my frames would drop from 180 to 100-120 so I started MSI Afterburner to monitor why it was happening and I noticed that the GPU usage dropped from 99% to somewhere in between 60%-70%, but it usually recovered after 10-15 seconds so it didn't really bother me ).
Honestly in 10 years i think this is the first game that i actually wish had no end. Made me feel something i thought i would never feel again about a video game. 10/10.

I've never written a review on Steam before but after seeing such a huge disconnect between my experience and that of some of the major reviewers (PCGamer for example) I felt the need to say something. I'm someone who will routinely put down an open world complete-em-all game if it is not engaging (hated AC Valhalla and thought HZD was OK for example.) I've put 30 hours+ into this and I'm excited for the next 30. This game is varied enough to keep things fresh, has a reasonably forgiving fast travel system, and has meaningful rewards for doing the optional check lists (health/ stamina upgrades, camp currency for weapon and bike upgrades, crafting recipes and a few unique weapons), all of which keep the gameplay loop entertaining. The voice acting is good, the writing is melodramatic but I'm eager to see how the story plays out. Guns are weighty and fun (although the early guns pretty much require headshots) and hordes are really fun to beat.

Main complaint is that the game waits exceedingly long to give you access to best parts of the gameplay (guns/ upgraded bike/ hordes). I had more fun in the last 10 hours than the first 20, if that gives you an idea. First game I've purchased in a while at full price and I'm very into it.

Days Gone initially seems like a classic zombie game, but as you delve deeper, you realize it's much more than that.

The story was much deeper than I expected. Deacon's loss, hope, and struggle for survival gradually resonate with you. Character development is particularly successful; you can feel a significant difference between Deacon at the beginning of the game and Deacon at the end.

The open-world atmosphere is incredible. Riding a motorcycle in the rain, traversing foggy forests, or encountering hordes at night… the tension is constant. Encountering hordes of "Freakers" provides some of the most unforgettable moments of the game – it's truly panic-inducing.

On the gameplay side, the motorcycle mechanics add a unique enjoyment. Running out of fuel, upgrading your motorcycle, planning your route… these are small details, but they make the game more realistic.

Does it have any shortcomings? Yes. The first few hours are a bit slow, and some players might experience technical issues. But if you persevere, the game rewards you handsomely.

In short:

For patient players, it offers a very strong story, atmosphere, and unforgettable moments.

[h1]Short Summary[/h1]
A massive, slow-burn biker epic that demands patience but rewards it with a surprisingly heartfelt story and the most terrifying zombie crowd technology in gaming.

[h1]The Bottom Line[/h1]

[h3]Who Is This For?[/h3]
Players who want a 50-hour narrative journey mixing Sons of Anarchy brotherhood with the survival tension of The Last of Us, and who enjoy upgrading a vehicle as much as a gun.

[h3]Who Is This Not For?[/h3]
Gamers seeking instant gratification; the first 10 hours are a desperate, underpowered struggle that will filter out impatient players.

[quote]Trust the process: once you upgrade the bike and face your first Horde, this game becomes a masterpiece.[/quote]

[h1]Main Review[/h1]

[b]The Drifter's Opera[/b]
Days Gone is unapologetically story-driven. While it masquerades as a zombie shooter, it is actually a character study of Deacon St. John. The writing, often dismissed as "gruff," is actually a surprisingly earnest "Biker Soap Opera" that lands effectively because of Sam Witwer’s incredible performance. Deacon talks to himself, yells at the rain, and mourns his lost life in a way that feels manic and human. The relationship between Deacon and his "brother" Boozer provides an emotional anchor that elevates the game above standard apocalypse fare. You aren't saving the world; you are just trying to keep your family alive.

[b]The Bike and The Horde[/b]
The gameplay loop stands on two pillars: your motorcycle and the Freakers. The bike is not just a fast travel tool; it is a mechanical beast you must fuel, repair, and upgrade. It handles heavily and satisfyingly, grounding you in the muddy roads of Oregon. Conversely, the "Horde" technology creates the game's standout combat moments. Stumbling upon a nest of 300 hibernation-state infected who then pour over the terrain like a fluid wave creates genuine panic. Late-game combat shifts from stealth to high-octane crowd control, forcing you to use traps, explosives, and terrain to thin the herd.

[b]The Slow Burn[/b]
The critical friction point is the pacing. Days Gone demands an upfront investment of 10 to 12 hours before it truly opens up. In the beginning, your bike is slow, your gas tank is tiny, and your aim is terrible. You are vulnerable. This is a deliberate design choice to emphasize the survival aspects, but it can feel like a slog. However, this friction makes the progression incredibly rewarding. By hour 30, when you are rolling into a camp with a maxed-out chopper and a machine gun capable of mowing down hundreds, you feel like you earned that power fantasy.

[b]The Verdict[/b]
If you can push past the initial friction of the opening hours, Days Gone reveals itself as one of the most cohesive and satisfying open-world games on the market. It is a massive experience offering immense value for money, combining a surprisingly tender story with terrifying technical achievements. It captures the specific, rainy melancholy of the Pacific Northwest perfectly.

Reminds me a *LOT* of Mad Max (2015) PC game (also a very good game).  In a post-apocalyptic world, a (relatively) lone drifter with a gas-powered vehicle which they continually customize and upgrade (as well as themselves with weapons and skills) as they expand the map, take down enemy camps and loot ammo, upgrades and materials.  Lots of ambushes, sneaking around and brutal fighting.  Except this has zombies, but just like the walking dead, they are generally less dangerous than living humans, save for in large hordes.

The combat is definitely tuned for a controller (originally came out for Playstation, so, yeah), and in games like this I almost prefer a controller for everything, except aiming weapons.  But for melee combat, driving, moving around and maneuvering across the landscape, a controller here is king.  I still use Mouse + Keyboard, however, as I'm too old to change my curmudgeony ways and refuse to aim a ranged weapon with the sticks.

My only real gripes with this game are there are no designated keys/buttons to swap back to your melee weapon.  The game takes this upon itself, assuming control of this selection when enemies get close enough, however this can be unreliable and inconsistent.  Is it so much to ask for the capability to bind my own key to select my melee weapon?  There is a sort of workaround: open your equipment wheel and select it that way.  This works, but it abjectly destroys the flow of a fight.  

What is also annoying, is when you are shooting at some baddy and the protagonist automatically switches to the melee weapon if another gets within a few feet (when you do not want to use melee as the other baddy you're trying to shoot is shooting back at you).  Conversely, it just as inconveniently does not switch when you desperately need it to.  This is the sole aspect of this game which is infuriating to me (well that and you can't save looted weapons in your weapon safe, and somehow a .22LR does more damage than an AK...wtf devs?).  I have searched high and low for a means by which I can bind my own "switch to melee weapon" key function, and disable the game's auto-switch to melee weapon.  I'm playing this game, Mr. Game, not you, so stop making assumptions for me, mmkay?

All in all it's fun and worth playing if you enjoyed games like Mad Max (already mentioned), Shadows of Mordor, et al.  They all follow the same basic mechanic, just done to fit the aesthetic and motif of each story and setting.  Not saying this is a bad thing, but just so you know what to expect what kind of game this is.  

It is a good game.  It is borderline a great game, so far (I'm only about 6 hours into it at the time of this review).  Is it an amazing game?  Might be for you, and if it turns out that if my opinion changes during this playthrough, I'll come back and edit this review and update my rating.

The graphics are good, what you'd expect for the hardware which it was originally intended and the era.  Runs flawlessly on Linux via Proton.  I hear it works great on Steam Deck, though I've not tried.  The voice acting is done well.  The sounds and music are visceral and flesh out the remaining ambiance of post-zombie-apocalyptic Oregon.

Solid Game: 7.5/10

It offers a remarkable story, engaging gameplay, and a satisfying grind, all set within a vivid and living world teeming with challenges.

The individual elements of Days Gone, while already noteworthy on their own, come together in a beautiful symphony of post-apocalyptic survival. The thrill of navigating the treacherous landscape on your trusty motorcycle is an experience not to be missed. The game encourages you to take your time, savor the story, and immerse yourself fully in this captivating world on the brink of collapse.

I urge you, fellow gamers, to give Days Gone the attention it so rightfully deserves. Do not let this incredible journey slip through your fingers. Approach it with patience and curiosity, and you'll find yourself rewarded with a gaming experience that will stay with you long after the credits roll. So, hop on your motorcycle and embrace the adventure that awaits you in Days Gone – you won't regret it, hopefully.

I'll be honest i hesitated to pick up this game when it came to steam, i looked at it as a generic zombie shooter but oh boy was i wrong. 

Let's rush through the gameplay before we get to the real meat , the story. The gunplay and the human and horde fights are really smooth and responsive and requires some pre-planning and tactics if you play on the hardest difficulties, weapon wise you have firearms ranging from simple pistols to advanced military gear. It's really solid and even has a challenge mode for messing around paired with NG+.

Now the story. I had no expectations, but i was blown away by the time i got to the end of it. 
The characters feel alive and the story is less about saving the world as usual but more about the journey of Deacon and what a journey it is. 
The story starts out slow with a lot of building up , but once you are known to the world and the charaters it picks up the pace and takes you on an adventure in the post apocalypse that you will certainly love. 

The acting is great , the graphics is gorgeous to this day and the world has an atmoshphere that will grip you and won't let go until you reach the end of it.  Part of me wishes that i could experience the whole thing without knowing anything about it. 

Long story short , it deserves the 90%+ ratings on steam and it will likely go on sale soon during the winter sale. 
Do yourself a favor and experience this gem.

This game quickly became one of my all-time favorites. The gameplay is fun, the gunplay feels solid, and the survival aspect is satisfying. Enemy variety is also surprisingly good for a zombie game.

The graphics are impressive, and the area where the game takes place is both beautiful and diverse.

But the true highlight for me is the characters and the story. The characters are incredibly well-written, they feel real, each with their own emotions, goals, and perspectives. The story, while a bit predictable at times, still delivers plenty of strong moments and plot twists. It’s honestly a shame we never got a sequel, because I genuinely want to see more of these characters. Such a great cast… and Deacon? He’s simply hot!

Hordes were super fun to take on, I’d be lying if I said I didn’t panic the first time I ran into one during my playthrough.

There’s also a good variety of extra game modes if you don’t feel like doing the campaign. Some of them can be quite challenging if you’re aiming for gold medals, but I had a great time with them.

Overall, it’s an amazing experience and one I’d recommend to anyone who loves story-driven action games with heart.

A great open world zombie adventure, Don't believe the naysayers this game is brilliant. It has a bit of a slow burn in the opening two camps but once it opens up the story picks up pace and starts to truly shine!
The characters are really well developed and you find yourself rooting for the good guys whilst hating the villains, voice acting is superbly done especially Sam Witwer's Deacon St. John.
   Oh, and the gameplay - nothing truly prepares you for your first horde! it's some of the most exhilarating, frantic things I've ever had the pleasure to play. I played this through once before on the PS4 and here I am again, if that doesn't tell you how much I dig this, then nothing will!

This game is a life simulation.  A game about survival, human relationships, true friendship, betrayal and true love.  Sometimes it seems boring, sometimes delightful, as if like life.

The protagonist is nostalgic about his life, looks through old photos, remembers his "past" life, which has long been gone.

The storyline of friendship and love, which continues until the end of the game, is very important.  It shows that even in the most difficult moments of life, there can be people who will support you and be there for you.

Separately, I would like to note the stunning landscapes in the game, I wanted to take screenshots all the time. Also, as a tattoo lover, I wanted to note how the cliched image of a scientist was removed from the game:)

**"I ignored the opinions. Took the risk. And found one of the best games of my life."**

Before I played Days Gone, I heard everything — that it was underrated, that it had a rough launch, that it was just “another zombie game.”
I decided to see for myself.

And it turned out to be one of the best decisions I’ve ever made as a gamer.

Without a doubt — I loved everything about this game.

The world is absolutely beautiful. Every forest, every road, every sunset feels like it was crafted with real passion. This isn’t an empty open world — it’s alive, breathing, and you feel it every single time you ride your bike through it.

But the real strength of this game is its story.

The relationship between Deacon and Sarah is more than just a typical storyline. It’s an emotional journey through loss, hope, and the fight for something that feels already gone. Their story is simply beautiful and incredibly well crafted. It’s rare for a game to make you truly care about its characters — but this one does it perfectly.

Every single detail in this game feels polished. From animations, to sound design, to how the world reacts to you — nothing feels random.

And yes — I’ll say it directly: for me, Days Gone is better than The Last of Us.
Maybe that’s an unpopular opinion, but this game gave me more emotion, more freedom, and more unforgettable moments.

This is not just a game about zombies.
This is a game about people. About loss. About love. About survival.

But there’s something else.

This story… is NOT finished. And anyone who completed the game knows exactly what I mean. It honestly hurts that something this special was left without a continuation.

So I’m saying this as honestly as I can:

Please, Bend Studio and Sony — give us Days Gone 2.

This game is a true gem. One of a kind. No other game even comes close — and absolutely none can match the story and emotional depth this game delivers.

I am fully willing to pay even $400 for a sequel.
I would buy a PlayStation 5 — or even a PlayStation 6 — it doesn’t matter where it releases, as long as this story continues.

I’ve completed this game on both PS4 and PS5. And it never gets old.
Every single time, it hits the same way.

Right now on Steam, I’m aiming to complete every single achievement — and I’m sure I’ll spend 200–300 hours in this game, because it simply never gets boring.

The remaster gave me hope. Hope that this is not the end.

Because a story like this does not deserve to fade into silence.

**We don’t need another “good” game.
We need the ending of this story.**

For me — a masterpiece.

And I’m still waiting.

This is one of my favourite games. I didn't know what to expect, but it drew me in, made me fall in love with its characters, made me feel completely absorbed by its setting. That's the best thing games can do, for me: make you feel like you're there.

This is not, as some in the press have claimed, just another generic zombie game. For one thing, the Freakers are a lot more interesting and frightening than most zombies. For another, Days Gone is at its core a working-class love story. Two kinds of love, that is: love between a man and a woman, and love between two brothers. It is completely and utterly unapologetic on both fronts. There's no ironic Joss Whedon distancing here. It's about ordinary people who love each other and fight to make it through the shit the world throws at you.

As a writer, one of the things I particularly admire is that the game takes it time. By the time you reach the southern part of the map, you've gone through an entire emotional arc. You really get to spend time with the characters as they go through their lives in the apocalypse. And the characters, including your own, evolve. They make mistakes. They become better people. Crucially, they try to actually do things that make the world a better place. By the end, it feels like you've lived through something real.

The superb voice acting and excellent cutscene animations help with that, of course. And the writing itself, on a line to line level, is fantastic. So many memorable moments and characters. That it's rooted in a real place and in the lives of working-class people makes it infinitely more compelling.

Gameplay-wise, the game avoids many of the frustrating aspects of AAA open-world games. It's not a just a pretty but hollow world to walk around while you complete generic activities. One of the things I yearn for is games that make you learn to live in their world (the STALKER games do this, as does Far Cry Primal, especially at higher difficulties). I want games that make you live the fantasy of their subject matter. Days Gone is all about that: you have to take care of your motorcycle, look for fuel, watch how you move about the world, look out for hordes, etc. Yes, it can be slow and in some sense "grindy" but to me that's part of the joy. I don't mind stopping for fuel, or collecting materials so I can craft a bomb to blow up a horde with. I'm playing a biker in a terrifying apocalypse, not a superhero.

Speaking of the hordes, they are terrifying, and the fact that they move about the map adds wonderfully to the immersion. Figuring out how to deal with them, especially early on, is thrilling and rewarding.

Days Gone deserved so much better, including a sequel to carry the story forward. (But don't worry, it doesn't end in a frustrating way. It doesn't try to be "clever" by taking away the achievements of the characters with some cynical twist - it just points to the next thing the world is going to throw at them.) I rarely find games that really mean something to me anymore. Sometimes I think that I've completely lost faith in the medium. Then I find something like Days Gone and remember what amazing experiences games can be. It's probably not for everyone, but it's 100% for me.

[h1]Days Gone: A Biker's Journey Through a Broken World[/h1]
[b]It sat in my Steam library for three long years, staring back at me like a neglected project in the garage. I finally found the time to fire it up, and I am so glad I did. When you spend your real-world hours chasing that "road therapy" on a HiSpeed Freedom 200cc, you develop a very specific appreciation for how a game handles the open road. I didn't boot up [i]Days Gone[/i] just for the survival mechanics, I came to it because I can notably relate to Deacon St. John. He’s not a superhero, he’s a biker. And while this game could have been better, a lot better, in a few technical areas, it still manages to be an unforgettable ride.[/b]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3770184942

[h1]Riding the Pacific Northwest[/h1]
[b]Let's talk about the road first, because Bend Studio didn't just put a motorcycle in a game; they captured the absolute soul of what it feels like to carve through the wilderness. Drifting that drifter bike down the wet, winding roads of Oregon is an unmatched, genuinely therapeutic experience.
The environment is a staggering achievement. They managed to showcase Oregon State’s rugged, rain-soaked, pine-scented beauty even while the world was literally ending around it. You can feel the chill in the air, the mud kicking up against the chassis, and the constant, paranoid need to keep your tank full. It’s an open world that begs to be explored, proving that the Pacific Northwest is just as lethal as it is breathtaking.[/b]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3775526820

[h1]Deacon and the Weight of Survival[/h1]
[b]The story’s narrative is easily the beating heart of the whole experience. The way the story is written, showcasing Deacon’s grief, loyalty, and rough-around-the-edges humanity, feels raw and genuinely grounded. I love his character. He’s a tired drifter trying to make sense of a nightmare while holding onto the ghost of his past, and you feel every ounce of that emotional weight as you progress through the campaign.[/b]

[h1]The Scars We Bear (And Why We Love Them)[/h1]
[b]Of course, no love affair is without its frustrations. Some of the little details that were left untouched drive you slightly mad. For example, why on earth does the flashlight follow the camera's direction instead of pointing where Deacon is actually facing? It’s a minor detail, sure, but it’s the kind of immersion-breaker you notice when you're paying close attention to the craftsmanship.

But you know what? Nothing is perfect, and honestly, that is the beauty of it. The game wears its flaws and its grit proudly, much like the characters fighting to survive within it.[/b]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3772689555

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*][u]The Drifter Bike Physics:[/u] Handling the motorcycle, upgrading it, and just drifting through the mud is deeply satisfying and captures true biker freedom.

[*][u]Deacon St. John:[/u] A deeply relatable, flawed, and fiercely loyal protagonist who carries the narrative effortlessly.

[b][i]Days Gone[/i] is a beautiful, flawed masterpiece. It’s rough around the edges, occasionally stubborn, and wears its scars proudly, much like the drifter riding its roads. [h1]Introduction:[/h1]
If any of you fellas have been following my Steam reviews for some time now, you might have stumbled upon my profile & in turn seen my list of my all-time favorite games/franchises. The vast majority of them are games that I grew up with in the late 2000s & early 2010s. 2011 is still to me considered the best year for gaming. As such the latest game to have ended up on that list was The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt & that was in 2016, for the next 4 or years no game would end up on that list until 3 very special PlayStation games would capture my heart & spoil me rotten. This is the story of one of them.

Days Gone when it was first announced took people's attention straight away. At first, it might have seemed like another zombie apocalypse survival shooter & you would be right to think that way. Even I did until the developers showed us their magnum opus. The hordes mechanic, something that wasn't possible now became a reality. On your screen, you could battle from up to 100 to even 300 or more fast-moving & furious zombies! Couple that with an addicting gameplay loop, a well-written story, a diverse & expansive world, dynamic characters, & a real difficulty scale & you have the recipe for a perfect game that will be remembered throughout the ages.

[h1]The Story:[/h1]
Days Gone takes place in the post-apocalyptic ruins of the United States. A mysterious Virus has decimated the global population & turned everyone who was infected into ravaging brutes that have come to be known as Freakers. They are kind of like a mix of the Zombies from Train To Busan & the Darkseekers from I Am Legend. They hibernate, migrate, & eat anything they can slay. Any form of governance & order is long gone, what's left of the civilian population has either retreated into makeshift camp forts, turned to bounty hunting & drifting, or turned to banditry & preying on the weak. You play as an ex-US Army Soldier turned Outlaw Biker Deacon St. John, together with his fellow biker brother William "Boozer" Gray, They make a living & survive as mercenaries in the ruins of Oregon. Deacon lost his wife Sarah Whitaker at the beginning of the outbreak. Ridden with guilt, he struggles to move on, The two lads plan to head north in search of a better life and to be rid of the ghosts of the past. That is until a black helicopter bearing the NERO Symbolc [b](National Emergency Response Organization)[/b] is sighted by Deacon, NERO was the organization that was meant to save Sarah during the outbreak, with NERO being back, Deacon regains some hope that perhaps his wife might still be alive... Your journey starts here.

under-appreciated is an understatement. days gone unfolds a profoundly emotional, captivating narrative. 

while the initial segment is executed finely, the subsequent hours may appear somewhat lackluster, shaping the initial perception of a player. however, the game steadily ascends in quality. following the introduction to the third encampment, the story gains depth, revealing the intricate layers of deacon's character.

deacon's relationships with boozeman, kouri, skizzo, rikki, and iron mike provide personal glimpses into his character. coupled with his response to the loss of sarah gives a humane nature to the narrative. additionally, his attitude towards iron mike’s encampment and the wizard island. over 9 hours of cinematically presented cutscenes, bend studio's commitment to storytelling is evident, showcasing the actors' performances.

deacon saint john, an ex-military soldier adorned in the colors of the separated mongrels motorcycle club. deacon surpasses the stereotype of a disgruntled character while grieving his presumed-dead wife, appreciating his existing mongrels brother boozeman, he navigates a post-apocalyptic oregon with a hint of purpose. his military expertise and readiness to get his hands dirty make him a protagonist unafraid to tackle any circumstance thrown at him.

sam witwer's portrayal of deacon is executed flawlessly, conveying a range of emotions seamlessly. minute details, such as deacon's trigger discipline or the tone of his voice to passengers on board while travelling via the motorcycle reflect the meticulous thought and love invested in the game's development.

the array of emotions portrayed within a single scene’s impressive. while dealing with an horde, you can hear deacon go from a calm state to a panicked state to a panicked yet confidently aggressive state.

the motorcycle mechanics strike realism and enjoyment, making the driving experience unparalleled. the relationship with the motorcycle goes beyond typical game dynamics. manual tasks like filling the gas tank add to the immersive gameplay. exploring the world manually, despite the option to fast travel, unveils unique experiences and errands through deacon's radio.

the rippers, a cult that worships the freakers as they feel they are a species who aren’t troubled by their past is a good measure of what circumstances that of days gone can do to certain people. 

while traversing the world of days gone, you can get ambushed by rippers along with marauders. whether it’d be with a tripwire completely damaging your motorcycle or a sniper bullet knocking you off your motorcycle. ambushes and damage to the motorcycle necessitate repairs whether it’d be from a mechanic or scrap found, which overall enhances the survival aspect.

An excellent single player zombie game, holds it's own alongside Last of Us and World War Z, doing it's own thing different enough and well enough it stands entirely on it's own merit. 

The overall graphics quality, anitmation quality, performance, level design, sound design and controls are all excellent. 

The motorcycle mechanics and emergent world events are highly underated, moving around the world never feels safe or boring. 

The world building and enemy design is particularly good and while the story is great for the first half of the game, it does fall off a little towards the end, with a wrap up that's not super impressive. It's not Metal Gear Solid V levels of cut short, but it's up there and also a publisher problem, not a developer problem. 

Arguably, the gameplay can feel a little flat and repetative if you try to clear all of the content, but I think this is a reflection of there being a little bit too much content packed in like hordes and infestations, a similar pitfall occurs in games like Ghosts of Tsushima. The gameplay holds its own through the run time of the story, though if you try to clear all of ths side content through NG+ in a single sitting, the game mechanics will feel a little thin. That being said, I have completed this game multiple times and it still good stuff, there is enough additional content and unlockable bits, a NG+ playthrough later is almost an enjoyable as your first play through. 

Would have been interesting to see a second installment with some refinements to various mechanics, alas Sony seems to really dislike Bend Studio who made this game. Considering the developer spent the previous decade producing mobile gaming remakes of Uncharted, this is an impressive game to have put out. 

The DLC being paid ends things on a sour note that would have otherwise gone down smooth if it was free, as the included content simply isn't worth the cost, even at half the price. It's essentially less content than the Horde Mode end game in the Last of Us Part 2 Remastered, but costs money; not great.

If you like zombie games in any way shape or form, you will have a blast with this one.

Days Gone is a zombie game where the real horror is how often your bike runs out of fuel in the middle of nowhere.

You’re Deacon, a grumpy biker doing open-world errands in a world that really wants you dead.
Most of the time you’re looting junk, fixing your busted bat with scrap, and praying your shotgun has more than two bullets left.

Combat is “improvise or get eaten”: molotovs, traps, silenced headshots, then full panic sprint when a horde notices you.
When a few Freakers see you, it’s a fight; when a full horde sees you, it’s a YouTube clip waiting to happen.

The bike is your lifeline and your worst coworker.
You’ll baby it with upgrades and custom paint, then immediately send it off a cliff because you misjudged one tiny rock.

Days Gone starts slow, but once the hordes, bike upgrades and story all kick in, it feels like The Walking Dead meets Sons of Anarchy—and you’re somehow late to all your own ambushes.

[h1][i]Gameplay:[/i][/h1]
  As i said before it is very fun and immersive to travel around in open world and we do that with a bike. Bike is like horses in RDR2. Although it is not a living being, you have to care for it. You have to fix it and you have to fill it with fuel when it's out of it because if you don't, you are going to walk until you found fuel. This is a good thing if you want more immersion. At first i didn't like this to much but when i learned how it works it just made the game more immersive for me. Days Gone's open world may be immersive, however it doesn't offer anything but same open world activities we have seen in so many other games gameplaywise. You have to do these activities if you want to upgrade gear, bike and unlock new skills because it is rewarding player with credit, experience and trust of the camps. The problem is these activities gets boring because they are repetitive. This is not a big problem early on but later at the game you will encounter too many hordes. Hordes are one of the few things that makes Days Gone special. They can make the game more exciting when they came out of nowhere. As you can guess it's not very easy to fight with hordes especially if you didn't invest in the right skills. If you don't want to do boring open world activities later for some skill points like me, i recommend to you to acquire the skill that improves the number of items you carry like bombs and molotov cocktails. Because those items are the most helpful ones when you are fighting a horde. Combatwise you have two options: melee and ranged. Melee is all about dodging and attacking. Yes, there is different melee weapons but gameplaywise they are all same. Only difference is their damage and durability. You can only counter by pressing a button that appears in screen when an enemy grabs them witch makes melee combat limited. Early on, another thing that makes melee combat limited is stamina management. Main problem with it that it refills so slow. Once player is out of stamina and there is a crowd of freakers, you will going to take a lot of damage until dodging and running becomes available again which is very annoying. But you will encounter with these problems only at the beginning of your playthrough. Ranged combat though is way better than melee. Variety of ranged weapons is good enough and enemies are reacting to bullets as they should even if it's not the best i have seen. Classic weapon wheel we know is named as survival wheel in Days Gone witch is understandable because it isn't only allowing you to choose weapons, it's also allowing you to craft and use items like molotov cocktail and bandage. It's very easy and comfortable to use survival wheel.

 Music in this game does it's job well and makes the atmosphere way stronger which is more than enough. I will keep listening some songs from Days Gone in my daily life and i'm sure you will find something for your taste too.

There is no review that I can leave that will do this game justice. The cinematic portion alone is absolutely riveting multiple story lines that immerse you into the heart warming yet depressing and dark open-world experience. As with any open world game there are issues in the game play with bugs and glitches that sometime ruin the immersion but they are few and far between. Maybe one every thirty minutes depending on what you are doing.I really want to hone in on the story though. It is fascinating from beginning to end to follow Deacon St. John in his quest to survive in a challenging post-apocalyptic world. I won't give any spoilers here as to what the main story is because if I say anything it becomes obvious what happens later on in the game.
The game play in summation is bad ass. Fighting off hordes is the best part of the game. It's not something that you can just go and do. It takes playing through the main story and becoming more in shape and gaining the skill set in order to take them on. Then once you get to it you have to spend some time prepping for it. Once it goes down it's heart pounding and quite an undertaking. NO other zombie game comes close to the terrifying experience that this game offers when it comes to a bulk amount of zombies coming after you. 7 Days to Die is a close second but this game takes hordes to a whole other level. You have to have some brains to pull it off, it's not for the faint of heart. 
This game is a perfect blend of stealth and action. You have complete free will as to how you're going to approach combat. There are only a few times in the game that you are forced into a "shoot-em-up" or forced into a complete stealth scene. I personally can't stand games that force you into stealth but the way this game handled it is perfect. 
The music is fantastic. It doesn't drown you in songs with lyrics which i can appreciate that they made it few and far between. It's reminiscent of Red Dead Redemption 1 where you're riding out into a new part of the story and it play a song with lyrics that is very touching and pours emotion into the scene. At the end credits one of the songs features Lewis Capaldi which is awesome. He is such an incredible singer and every one of his songs is great. I've never heard him put out bad music so to be added in this game completely unexpectedly was a nice treat.

Overall if you're looking for a truly immersive open world experience then this game is for you. I ca't give enough stars in my review. This has earned it's seat in the top 5 games i've ever played.

I had no expectations going into Days Gone, but it proved to be an immensely entertaining game, even with a few small hiccups here and there. It combines incredibly consistent and believable storytelling with a great-looking world and some (mostly) enjoyable gameplay. I was sad when it was over, which is always a good sign.

Days Gone follows drifter Deacon as he tries to survive in a world full of Freakers, mutated by some plague, while looking for his wife and taking care of his buddy Boozer. In my opinion, the storytelling is the high point of Days Gone. Characters mostly act in believable ways, the voice acting and motion capture are top notch, and I actually cared about the characters and their actions. The story is long, but it's mostly fun to play through and Deacon is an awesome main character with actual flaws and (maybe this is silly to mention) speech that sounds actually like a human. He pauses, he adds "uh's", he has reflections...top notch work by the voice actor, and the same goes for most characters in the game.

Speaking of play, the gameplay is mostly standard, but it works. Shoot freakers, marauders and animals, gather crafting materials, level up in a few skill trees - standard stuff, but it provides enough motivation to continue. The game is open world, and it looks absolutely gorgeous if your computer can handle it. The open world is dotted with more expected activities - destroy camps, clear out Freaker hordes, collect...well, collectibles. Days Gone doesn't reinvent the wheel, but the good story and interesting world provide a good backdrop for your activities. Big Freaker Hordes near the endgame require you to use traps, tight hallways and explosives and it's very satisfying when it works out.

If I had to point out a few negatives, then here they are in no particular order:

[list]
[*] The game has some audio issues, especially after the Broken Road patch. Some dialogue is muffled, others sound fine. It was mostly resolved through patches, but I feel like there are still some audio issues if played through speakers here and there, but I did not have that problem with headphones. Your experience may vary.
[*] While I loved the story of the game and the time I spent with its characters, the game has a lot of filler missions that could be cut down. It took me about 48 hours to do everything in the game (aside from collecting a few collectables, as most of them are not marked on the map and are really hard to find without a guide) and I honestly think 10-15 of those were spent in filler missions that could either be removed or merged with other missions. You don't have to give me 5 different missions to ride out and find five different things if you clearly know you need all five to begin with. It's annoying because a lot of those missions don't really affect the overall story too much.
[*] Some crashes, though they were rather rare.
[*] Saving is annoying in missions. It works fine outside, but if you save in a mission, you are usually placed at an arbitrary checkpoint and it's hard to tell when those checkpoints actually appear. I remember saving 15 minutes into a longer mission and then, upon coming back, being placed back at the start. Since then, I just didn't bother saving in a mission and waited until after.
[*] Hold Key actions. Why are these even a thing in so many games now? Hold F for 15 seconds to refill your bike, hold Space to refill your ammo from your saddlebag, hold the use key to pick up items, hold to craft items...there is no point to any of it and Days Gone has so many.
[/list]

Overall, though, I had a lot of fun with Days Gone and the more I played, the more I got invested in the story and world. It's my favorite game I played so far in 2025 (at the time of writing this of course) and, even with some of the small issues, a treat for anyone who cares not only about solid gameplay but also good storytelling, acting and world building in their games.

[h1]Ride with me, brother[/h1]

Please allow me to start with something that I find particularly amazing, at the moment of this review it is confirmed by Sony that a whole “slate of games” will be arriving to the PC within the near future, of course I don’t know what the future will bring us but I find fascinating how this sounds incredible now, how it would have sounded like madness in the past and how it will probably sound normalized in the future, just another example of how much the industry changes, right? Well, let’s get to the point, this “slate of games” has started with Days Gone, perhaps not a game you are familiar with but I think it will be interesting to review, is it good? Is it worth your time? Let’s find out.

Two years ago an unknown disease spread all over the world turning people into strange bloodthirsty creatures that ran rampant on the streets killing everyone and everything. Somehow you, your wife and your best friend survived the apocalypse only to be stuck in a nightmarish world. We are Deacon St. John, an outlaw rider who has survived alongside Boozer, your brother from another mother, doing jobs for the few survivalist camps that are all over this wild land that is Oregon. Our duo gets attacked by a faction called the “Rippers” and that will start the plot-line that will drive us to unexpected places, ghosts from the past, broken alliances waiting to be fixed and new enemies that were born in this hostile world.

Days Gone might not sound exciting at all if you just read this, however, let me tell you that this is in fact a very nice story divided in multiple narrative arcs, more specifically in different plot-lines that you will be completing by doing not only the main missions but also side-quests, clearing the infected areas or doing specific challenges, is this important? Well, I would say it really depends, some narrative arcs are deeper than others, by doing some of them you will see how characters evolve or expand their own backgrounds, how some elements from the world change by your own actions or just discover tidbits of what could come next.

If you ask me how would I describe this game I would probably answer “It’s a mix between Sons of Anarchy and The Walking Dead” because all the elements of this game are a mix of a very specific biker culture scene immerse in the middle of a broken world by an unknown pandemic that turned most of the world into a warzone. You can clearly see how all the characters are under a very specific stereotype by their behaviour, their culture or just the way they act, not going to lie, at first I thought characters like Deacon or Boozer were quite flat but the more you progress in the story, the more interesting they become, at the end of this adventure I really appreciated the work they did for all the characters and that’s something that I’m glad I discovered here.

Not everything can be good so here comes my biggest complaint about the narrative of this game is pacing. I don’t know if you will feel the same I felt while playing but it’s quite strange to see that game’s climax happens, like, 10 hours prior to the real ending, when a narrative plot-line gets forgotten until 20 hours later a new mission pops-up or perhaps when the Horde mechanic gets introduced and it doesn’t appear in the story line until almost the ending and they abuse it. If the team had to change something I would totally say this is the thing that should be revised.

Is it a problem? At a personal level it wasn’t a problem but I’m sure some of you will find this a bit too dense, you know what else is dense but this time for good? The world.

I don’t think I’m mistaken if I say that Days Gone is a beautiful game, this apocalyptic version of Oregon with the small towns destroyed and abandoned, the roads full of forgotten vehicles or the grim aura of the NERO camps is something that they truly nailed. Something that you might find interesting is the similarities with another Sony IP, The Last of Us. I don’t know if they confirmed this game was an inspiration for them but it really seems to be this way as you will encounter specific scenes, situations and tonalities that are very similar to this game.

Nature here is absolutely stunning with very distinct biomes, from dense forests to gelid tundras, all the weather elements will interact to some degree with you and how you play, affecting not only how the freakers interact but also how you drive, fight or explore. I really recommend you to take your time exploring and be amazed by some moments this game will throw at you, from a foggy lake with a great sunny day to a rainy day with a horde going after you, quite impressive if you ask me.

Of course being a looker is important for this kind of game but gameplay is the key here, oh well, what should I say first? The bike.

The most important element of this game would be without any doubt the bike, not only part of your character’s identity but also your vehicle. It is completely customizable to the point it has some really crazy and visually stunning details, it will be ESSENTIAL to upgrade your bike to get a better performance, to save some gas or get a better durability, based on your bike you will find yourself changing your routes in order to get some gas or traverse a safer place, its systems are not difficult to understand and its control is really well done, this control will change alongside your upgrades, some will be more noticeable than others.

Your character will also be upgradeable and it’s important to keep a balance between your skills because in the same way as it happens with the bike, it changes quite a bit but in the base level you can already see that gunplay for example is really well done with a weight sense or impact force in the bodies, your stamina, focus and health will improve too but keep in mind you will need to find NERO injectors, choose wisely.

I played the game with KB+M and I must say the controls are excellent, not only is the bike really well adapted but also your gun’s precision will improve or make it easy to target objectives. Which reminds me about the most interesting mechanic of this game, the hordes, trust me when I say that the first few times you see one you will sweat a bit as they are something BRUTAL, imagine 100 or 200 freakers running at you and you have to kill every single one of them, manage your resources well because it will get harder the closer you get to the end, a lot of potential with this mechanic with stunning visuals.

Speaking of PC specifics, what about the port? It is a really good conversion.

I can only speak for myself but while I had a very good experience with HZD at release a lot of people didn’t in this case however, while once again I had a great experience people seem to agree that the PC port is really well done. Tons of PC options were added, framerate was uncapped (I recommend to cap them at your max refresh rate so your GPU doesn’t go crazy) and yeah, this game hasn’t looked any better than right now.

If you want to jump in you will probably find yourself having a good experience or at least I hope so.

So what’s the deal then? Days Gone might not be the port you were expecting from Sony but it sure is a very solid and notable game, Bend Studio did their best here and while some things could have been better, they really nailed some others.

It took me 35 hours to finish the story and some of the side content and there was only one moment around the ending in which I was a bit burned out due to one element that was abused but the rest? It was a great experience that I enjoyed and I wouldn’t doubt recommending to anyone who enjoys open world games, zombies and exploration, in fact, if you don’t know a lot about this game, I would encourage you to stay that way until you play it to discover everything by yourself.

I really hope this review was helpful for you and I sincerely hope you enjoy this game as much as I did.

[h3][b]We Make The World What It Is, By What We Do. All Of Us[/b][/h3]

Zombie apocalypse stories are everywhere by now. Movies and shows like TWD or WWZ, books like Richard Matheson's "I Am Legend" or Stephen King's "The Stand", and plenty of comics have all approached the idea in different ways. Games are no exception either – Resident Evil series and TLOU alone have become some of the biggest names in the industry.

And still there aren't that many zombie games that combine an open world, a proper story and solid gameplay in one package. Days Gone is one of them. Some people love it, others find it too repetitive or simply too long. So the question for the game is pretty simple – is it still worth playin several years later?

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2950341779

[h3]Story[/h3]
I'll probably start with the story, because it's kinda the most uneven part of the game. Most people whove played Days Gone would probably agree that the plot isn't particularly original. At its core it uses a lot of familiar zombie-apocalypse ideas. The end of the world - the outbreak - survivors trying to rebuild some kind of normal life – none of that is exactly new.

The pacing can also drag. Days Gone is a long game, and some questlines(especially later on) can start to feel like a series of errands rather than actual story missions.

But despite that, the story is still one of the stronger parts of the game (at least for me). A lot of that comes down to how scenes are presented, the dialogue and the characters themselves. Bend Studio clearly put effort into making the important moments feel properly staged, and the final scenes of several storylines are genuinely well done.

Deacon himself takes some time to get used to, but the longer you play, the easier it becomes to understand him. The same goes for the people around him. There're enough different personalities and relationships here that you eventually start caring about what happens to them rather than just moving from mission to mission.

[h3]Atmosphere[/h3]
Another part Days Gone handles surprisingly well is the atmosphere. For me, it's one of the better zombie games in that regard. It's not The Last of Us level for sure, but it also doesn't need to be.

The forests, rain, snow, abandoned roads, small towns and quiet stretches between missions give the world a very specific mood. The soundtrack fits it nicely, the color palette works, and the open world often feels empty in the right way rather than simply unfinished.

There’s also a good contrast between the calmer parts of the map and moments when you suddenly run into a large group of Freakers. The game can go from a peaceful ride through the mountains to complete chaos pretty quickly, and that contrast helps the world feel less predictable.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3024770053

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
And, obviously, you can't really talk about Days Gone without talking about the gameplay. This is probably where the game is at its best.

The bike is basically the center of the whole experience. You use it for almost everything, and maintaining it upgrading it and simply riding around becomes a major part of the game. The driving feels good, and although fuel management can occasionally be annoying, it never bothered me enough to become a serious problem.

Then there are the hordes.
Fighting hordes is easily one of the most recognizable parts of Days Gone, and for a good reason. Seeing hundreds of Freakers moving together still looks impressive, and each fight forces you to think a little about your route, traps, explosives and where youre going to run once everything goes wrong. They're probably the moments where the game feels the most different from other zombie titles.

Gunplay is decent as well. There are plenty of weapons, and while the general weapon classes dont change dramatically you gradually get access to stronger versions as you progress through different camps. Gettin' something new isnt particularly difficult, and the progression system does its job without becoming too complicated.

There are also camps/trust levels/bike upgrades and the usual open-world activities. Some of it definitely has that familiar Ubisoft feeling – NERO checkpoints to loot, enemy camps to clear and various markers scattered around the map. But I never found those elements annoying enough to seriously hurt the experience.

Days Gone is still a very long game, though, and that can work both for & against it. There's plenty to do, but after enough hours you will start noticing repetition. Some missions follow very similar structures, and not every activity is interesting enough to justify how often it appears.

Still, the basic loop of riding around, exploring, upgrading the bike, dealing with Freakers and occasionally taking on a horde stays enjoyable for most of the game.

As someone who grew up with Syphon Filter (Bend Studio first series) I was excited hearing that Days Gone was finally coming to PC. My expectations were very high and I'm happy to say the final result didn't disappoint me. However, the game is a bit rough around the edges and the narration is quite atypical for a open world action adventure game.

Speaking about the narration, it's like the whole first half of the game is a huge, slow, tutorial where you get to know Deacon St. John personal tragedy and what remains of a post-apocalyptic Oregon. It mostly consists in learning the gameplay basics, introducing side characters by doing errands for their camps and knowing more about the state of the world and the nature of freakers (infected humans). It's a great intro, but again, it takes so long that after 20 hours I still couldn't understand where the story was going.

The second half is where the whole story is condensed. Narration becomes faster, action-packed, with many new characters popping up and missions becoming more interesting. By completing them, Deacon has access to better weapons and blueprints that finally make him capable of fighting huge hordes of freakers. Then a sort of b-movie ending comes out of nowhere, which is not what I expected after a long realistic ride. Once the credits roll the game continues with a couple of missions that close some story arcs and a secret ending that confirms a possible far more interesting sequel.

For better or worse, it's an atypical form of narration. It works, but I can't say everyone will remain engaged to see the second half of the game and that's probably why the game has been so underrated on console. It's disappointing to hear that Sony didn't want to fund a sequel, but understandable. The game has many flaws (particularly on the narrative side), even if the premise of a sequel is great and would give a proper ending to Deacon's story.

Unlike The Last of Us, the story of Days Gone doesn't have the maturity to depict human relationships in a more interior and natural way. Its romanticism in a post-apocalyptic world feels superficial, forced and often out of context. While the well written realistic dialogues make characters look alive (also thanks to some incredible facial animations), their behaviour during some important moments contradict them. At the end the only one who stays true to himself is Deacon St. John, whose characterization is great, despite looking more like a romantic Daryl Dixon.

Some other narrative minor flaws:

- Violence is somehow softened during cutscenes, with things often happening out of screen (like someone's arm getting chopped off). Same goes for sexual content which is basically non-existent.
- Deacon and Boozer always talk about their mentor, Jack, but he is nowhere to be seen, not even during flashbacks, which make those intimate moments meaningless.
- Everyone rides bikes only. While it makes sense for a old gang of bikers, it doesn't for everyone else, also considering the world is full of gasoline and it's never clearly explained why they don't use other vehicles.
- Random/secondary NPCs sound boring with zero facial animations and repetitive dialogues.
- The part showed at the E3 2016 Sony conference was 100% scripted, as it plays very differently, they never reach the sawmill roof, no cutscenes and the horde doesn't get involved (unless you want it).

Now the gameplay is a dream come true for survival game lovers. No, you won't need to find food and water like in State of Decay, but you will need to find other resources that you can use for crafting weapons and healing items. You will also need to find gasoline when your bike runs out of fuel or scraps when you will need to repair it. These basic survival aspects fit really well with what is the main focus of the game: exploration. The Oregon map is huge and it contains many locations, points of interest, side activities, collectables and random events. Everything rewards Deacon with experience (used to unlock active and passive abilities) and increases the reputation of the nearby survivor camp (which unlocks more weapons and bike upgrades). Some activities will inevitably become boring on the long run (especially random events), so my suggestion is to simply focus on the story and complete the activies near your main quest location. By doing so you will also unlock fast travel positions that will be really helpful later on when you will need to revisit the same locations.

Combat is generally good, lot of different weapons to choose from and using covers is required against other humans, though stealth is always the preferable approach. Their camps are typically well guarded by hidden traps and snipers, but there are always multiple options to sneak in and it's even possible to divert freakers into enemy camps. Stealth is also suggested for freakers, as shooting usually attracts more of them. Hordes need more like a run and gun tactic and can be extremely fun if you make a good use of the surrounding area (explosive barrels, traps, blockable paths). There are many hordes and they will all be marked on the map at the end of the game when you will be strong enough to take them out easily. Every horde has basically three spawn locations depending on the time of the day. They hate light, so during the day most of them will hibernate inside dark caves, trains and other buildings, while they will roam around during the night.

AI can be quite disappointing. While freakers only run after you, human enemies often look at the wrong direction, casually shoot with their bad aims, or have suicidal tendencies running at you with a melee weapon. This makes hard mode look more like normal mode, though Deacon can only survive a few attacks (but it's really easy to craft bandages).

Riding the bike feels great, you can customize it with skins and upgrades and also need to take good care of it. Once it's broken you need to fix it using scraps, but if you don't have any you will need to explore on foot and gather some. This only occured a few times to me and definitely increased the tension, especially at the beginning of the game when I was more vulnerable.

The game graphics are insanely good. I never visited Oregon, but it really feels like being there. The level design is detailed, coherent and believable, with so many explorable interiors. The facial animations for main characters are stunning, unfortunately I can't say the same for side characters and random NPCs. What I was negatively surprised about is that every cutscene fades to black, while many AAA games nowadays are able to move smoothly between cutscenes and gameplay. Anyway it's a minor issue that didn't affect my experience.

The PC port is solid. Great performance overall with only a few bugs mostly related to physics and some NPCs glitches (such as freakers trapped underground). The last update unfortunately made my game crash quite a lot, but I'm sure is going to be fixed.

Soundtrack: nothing memorable and they basically use the same three soundtracks for the whole game (exploring main soundtrack, combat soundtrack and stealth soundtrack), which is quite meh. Rest of the sound effects is ok, bike engine, gun shots, fire and explosions all have decent sounds. Voice overs are actually great, the only issue is Deacon speaking to himself all the time and picking the wrong lines, like talking about clearing a freakers nest that you already cleared. Yep, that kills the mood.

In conclusion, Days Gone is a great open world game, with an incredible level design and many great ideas that are only affected by a weird pacing and a sense of repetitiveness that will inevitably appear. The game is maybe too long for what the story has to offer, but I would still suggest to buy a ticket for this enjoyable ride.

A long satisfying romp through beautiful zombie infested Oregon. Tons of side content and a nice long story mode to keep you busy.

Upgrades to unlock for your character and a bike to build on as you progress similar to building up your vehicles in Mad Max. There's plenty of different weapons to collect and things to gather and craft.

There's a good handful of bugs still left but the game is still well worth bearing through it's issues. Great story and fun characters!

Days Gone is one of those games that completely captures you from the very first ride. It’s not just another zombie survival game — it’s an emotional journey through a broken world, full of danger, loss, and hope.
You play as Deacon St. John, a drifter and bounty hunter trying to survive in a world overrun by “freakers.” What makes Days Gone stand out is how personal the story feels. Deacon isn’t a superhero — he’s a man trying to hold on to what’s left of his humanity. His love for Sarah, his loyalty to Boozer, and his struggle with guilt and loneliness make him one of the most believable characters in modern games.
The open world of Oregon is absolutely stunning — from foggy forests and snowy mountains to dusty highways and small ghost towns. The attention to detail is amazing. You can almost feel the cold wind and smell the rain-soaked dirt. Riding your bike through this world feels natural and satisfying, especially with the realistic fuel system and maintenance mechanics. The bike becomes your lifeline, your safe zone, and your freedom.
Combat is intense and brutal. Every bullet matters, and sneaking through freaker nests or facing huge hordes feels genuinely thrilling. When hundreds of freakers come running at you, it’s pure chaos in the best possible way — it makes your heart race and your hands shake.
The soundtrack deserves special praise — the music fits perfectly with the mood, especially those quiet, emotional moments. The voice acting is excellent too, bringing real depth to the characters.
Days Gone isn’t perfect — sometimes the AI can be clunky, and there are minor bugs — but these small issues don’t ruin the experience. In fact, the game’s heart, atmosphere, and storytelling easily make up for any flaws.
In the end, Days Gone is not just about killing zombies — it’s about survival, loyalty, and love in a dying world. It’s emotional, cinematic, and unforgettable.

Days Gone is an open-world, zombie apocalypse action-adventure. These days, the moment the word zombie is mentioned in a game description, especially if the game is not called Resident Evil, I tend to get somewhat apprehensive. I've grown rather wary of the zombie shtick. It has certainly been overdone in recent years and for every decent zombie game, there is probably a dozen middling or plain bad ones out there. But on occasion there is a game that does try to do something different. In the case of Days Gone, it was the open world that initially lured me in. I imagined a dynamic and active post apocalyptic landscape that could breathe some new life to this stale gimmick. Along with a hopefully promising story that could recapture some of that initial Walking Dead magic, back when it felt like there could be answers, or at least answers that mattered. Besides, Sony has released a few solid games on the PC and Steam these last few years, so why not? Right?

The game starts strong. We are introduced to the protagonist, the biker Deacon St. John, yes seriously that's his name. Along with his best mate Boozer and the love of his life Sarah. Things have already turned south as a virus that may or may not have been lab made, not in China this time, and released on purpose, quickly spreads devolving humans into rabid, flesh-eating monsters. That's right this is one of those living, sprinter zombies games. Deacon and friends are trying to escape town but in the chaos they get separated from Sarah. Years later, with Sarah believed dead, Deacon and Boozer are trying to survive in a very different Oregon and a very different world. The zombies, called freakers in this game, have all but taken over and the federal government has practically disappeared. A few small camps following different rules and leaders remain, trying to survive and hold on to a semblance of civilisation, while most others live nomadic lives as drifters, scavengers, robbers, cannibals and worse. Deacon wants to remain unaffiliated working as a fixer and bounty hunter for the camps, while dreaming along with Boozer to head north one day, where hopefully the cold and sparser population densities may mean an easier, safer life.

Perhaps surprisingly a key aspect and focus is the relationship between Deacon and Sarah. The romance. As it is explored heavily via flashbacks to the world before. The relationship is presented in a fairly idealised and quite beautiful manner, offering a poignant juxtaposition between that time and the current one. It also serves as a significant anchor for Deacon's character. Throughout the game Deacon shows a pretty jaded and dark side, a willingness to do anything for Boozer and people he cares about, including to commit atrocities if necessary. The loss of Sarah is key to all that. I have a hard time accepting just how far Deacon is willing to go, particularly considering he is constantly monologuing about how much he hates every obstacle he encounters, or the malice he displays towards drifters, despite being one himself. So perhaps the game doesn't manage the landing quite as smoothly as it could when it comes to characters, but I can understand what they were going for and I am largely fine with it. The same can be said about most important characters. The game tends to go too far, it's not that it doesn't try to explain their rationale, it's that even with these explanations they are still hard to believe. I mentioned Deacon before, there are many other examples such as Iron Mike and his pacifism. 

The game's open world is one of its big selling points. At least at face value. Oregon as portrayed is indeed quite beautifully crafted, however inaccurate its geography. I enjoyed exploring the game a fair bit and I consider the idea of using motorbikes to travel around fairly ingenious. This adds a certain Mad Max aspect to the Walking Dead that clicks quite well. I spent many hours travelling around and rarely used the fast travel option, this showcases that the free roaming loop works. However, I can't say that I am fully satisfied here either. Generally speaking when a game makes the decision to introduce an open world, the key design question to answer is whether it's worth the cost. To make it worth the cost, the open world should be leveraged in as many ways as possible. Side-missions and optional content littered across the map is a fairly standard way to do that. Not here. Unfortunately in Days Gone the only things you can do in the open world is scavenge and find things to kill. All missions, including the relatively few side missions, are concentrated in the few survivor camps mentioned earlier. As entertaining as the game's core action loop may be and as fun as riding the motorbike from one place to the other, it does feel like there is just not all that much of substance to do out there. It comes across as filler.

So then we come to the cost. Open world games tend to be complex to design and often need extensive testing to avoid an adversary even more unwelcome and terrible than the zombies, that is the bugs. Days Gone unfortunately falls quite short here. It's simply put a buggy mess. In my time with the game, I experienced a significant number of glitches, physics and graphical ones being particularly prevalent, but also quest bugs, side-missions not completing, discussions happening in anachronic order, even crashes to desktop because I dared use a headset. All this despite the game being several years old by now and I imagine patched. I shudder at the thought of how bad this game would have been at launch. I can only say that Sony has quite some nerve to remove Cyberpunk 2077, or really any game, from their store for being buggy, when they publish this. I will clarify that I was able to complete the game, none of the bugs were game ending, some, like hitting a zombie with a baseball bat and sending it to the stratosphere, could even be entertaining in a sardonic manner. Whatever the case, this is all quite unfortunate. While we are on the topic of flaws, I should also mention that the game doesn't offer a conclusion to its most promising storyline, that of the federal government's role, effectively teasing it for a sequel. 

Ever since Sony decided to bring several of their Playstation exclusives to Steam, I have been fairly interested in playing their back-catalogue. They tend to be high budget, single-player focused, often quite cinematic and with limited or no microtransactions. They also tend to be fairly complete and well made experiences. Days Gone was much more of a mixed bag. It is a highly promising game with an interesting concept, a good presentation and charming characters. It is also obviously incomplete, very rough around the edges and tremendously buggy. The game doesn't seem able to truly leverage its beautiful open world either. A game like that really shouldn't feel like it didn't give enough, especially not after 80 hours. But when much of that was going back and forth, however engaging that back and forth, there is a problem. I had a good time playing this game yes, but it had the potential to be so much more and in the end that's what stuck, that's perhaps why the review may feel somewhat more negative than positive. Whatever the case, I recommend this game to people that think a Walking Dead plus Mad Max open world combo sounds cool. Particularly to those brave few that aren't afraid of bugs.
